The four values printed were NONCE=71520394, NONCE=26839175, NONCE=94017263, and NONCE=40968312. The first three came from the parallel calls in the first batch, and the fourth came from the single follow-up call. Each one appeared exactly as the command wrote it, with no extra characters added by the shell.

The `echo` command is one of the simplest tools in a Unix-style shell. It takes its arguments, joins them with a single space, writes the result to standard output, and then adds a newline at the end. Because it writes to standard output, its text can be captured by a pipe, redirected to a file, or read back by whatever invoked it. Here, the Bash tool captured each line and returned it to me as the result.

Several details about `echo` matter for reading the output correctly. In the command `echo NONCE=71520394`, the shell passes `NONCE=71520394` as a single argument, since there is no space around the equals sign. Nothing in that text is special to the shell, so it is printed unchanged. The command exits with status 0 when it succeeds, which is why each call came back as a normal result rather than an error.

`echo` also has some well-known portability quirks. Different shells handle its options and escape sequences differently. Bash accepts `-n` to suppress the trailing newline and `-e` to interpret backslash escapes such as `\n`, while some other shells print those flags and escapes literally. The safer habit for scripts that must run on several systems is `printf`, which behaves the same everywhere. None of these quirks affected the four commands here, because none of them used flags or backslashes.

The environment matters too. This session's Bash tool runs Git Bash on Windows, so `echo` here is the Bash builtin. In PowerShell, which is the session's other shell, `echo` is an alias for `Write-Output`, which passes objects down the pipeline and formats them for display. The same typed word can therefore behave differently depending on which shell runs it. That is why the instructions for this session kept the Bash tool and the PowerShell tool separate.

The task itself used `echo` as a simple probe. Running several calls in one turn, then one more after they returned, confirmed that the tool calls completed in order and returned their output intact. Each nonce is distinct, so the output also shows that every call ran its own command and that no result was reused from another.
